title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
hook: the sky is dark with clouds, and Radha is told to take him home

segments.voice: Yesterday, puja: a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water, and the whole year of service laid on the tray as an offering.
screen: `A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.`

segments.voice: The sky is heavy with clouds. The forest is dark with tamala trees. Night is coming on, and the boy is nervous. So Nanda, the cowherd chief, turns to Radha: take him home. That's how the Gita Govinda begins, with a walk home through the dark. And the verse hails what follows on the bank of the river Yamuna: the secret love of Radha and Madhava, one of Krishna's names. After our days on the Bhagavad Gita, the path turns from Krishna the teacher on a battlefield to Krishna the beloved in a forest.
screen: `CLOUDS, DARK TREES, NIGHT.` → `TAKE HIM HOME.` → `FROM BATTLEFIELD TO FOREST.`

segments.voice: Gita Govinda means the song of Govinda, the cowherd, another name for Krishna. It's a love poem, and it says so up front. A few lines in, Jayadeva gives an invitation. If your heart is moved by remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to these sweet, soft, lovely words of Jayadeva. Both conditions in one sentence: remembering God and the play of lovers, offered as a single door. That pairing is the heart of what the poem means by bhakti. The word means devotion, loving attention, and in the Gita we just finished, Krishna praised it as a way to him. Here bhakti stops being a teaching and becomes a song. Before the love story starts, though, Jayadeva sings a hymn through the Lord's descents into the world, the avatars: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and on through Rama and the Buddha to Kalki, one stanza each. Every stanza ends with the same refrain: jaya jagadisha hare, victory to you, Hari, Lord of the world. So the reader meets the cosmic Lord first, the one who saves worlds in many forms, and only then the timid boy Radha is walking home under the clouds. The poem holds both at once. In the stories to come, Radha's longing for Krishna, and his for her, are read by some devotees as the soul's longing for God and God's for the soul. Jayadeva doesn't explain that; he just sings.
screen: `THE SONG OF GOVINDA, THE COWHERD.` · `REMEMBERING HARI, AND THE ARTS OF LOVE.` · `A HYMN TO THE LORD'S DESCENTS.` · `THE COSMIC LORD, THEN THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `JAYA JAGADISHA HARE.`

segments.voice: Hear the opening again, clouds, dark trees, night coming, someone asked to walk another home, and let your mind find a person you've walked home in some way: driven, waited with, stayed on the phone with until they were safe. Breathe with that memory. If you pray, you can let the refrain move quietly with the breath, jaya jagadisha hare; if not, just stay with the picture of two figures walking under the clouds.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda, it's sung: remembering Hari and the play of love, through one door.
Your line: take him home. Tomorrow, spring, and Radha at the edge of the dance. That's day nine hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Songs from the Gita Govinda are sung in Hindu devotional settings and performed in classical music and dance, and the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare is sung on its own as well.

chat.says: Why does a Hindu devotional poem read like a love story?
options: Jayadeva offers remembering Hari and the play of love as one door: bhakti.
It's just entertainment; the poem never really mentions God at all.
Because Krishna gave up being God to live as an ordinary cowherd.
chat.meaning: Jayadeva invites those moved by remembering Hari and curious about love: both through one door. That pairing is the heart of bhakti here.

Gita Govinda.meaning: the song of Govinda: Jayadeva's love poem of Radha and Krishna

Jayadeva.meaning: the poet who wrote the Gita Govinda

Nanda.meaning: the cowherd chief who raised Krishna

Yamuna.meaning: the river beside Krishna's cowherd village

Radha.meaning: the cowherd girl Krishna loves in the Gita Govinda

notes: Editor: hook no longer says the love 'begins' on the walk (the verse hails the secret love-play on the Yamuna bank); 'Devotees hold both at once' (a claim about all devotees) changed to a statement about the poem.
No date is given for Jayadeva or the poem, per the claims rule.

Opening verse (meghair meduram ambaram...) is paraphrased; who speaks the instruction is traditionally read as Nanda; confirm. The verse's sense of the boy being 'timid' (bhirur ayam) rendered as 'nervous'.
Verse numbering: the invitation (yadi hari-smarane sarasam mano...) is given as 1.3; confirm numbering in the edition used.

The avatar list in the teach stops at Rama ('and on through Rama') and does not number the forms, per the claims rule; the hymn later names Balarama, the Buddha and Kalki. A Keeper may choose to list them.
'Read by some devotees as the soul's longing for God': a soft general claim; confirm.
Edwin Arnold's 'The Indian Song of Songs' (1875) is a public-domain version, but no wording was quoted from it.

Audit 2026-10-01: fixed a reversal in the teach ('the young man walking a girl home'): in 1.1 Radha is told to take the timid boy, Krishna, home. The avatar line no longer implies the hymn ends at Rama; it now runs on through the Buddha to Kalki (forms still not counted).
